evidence: The manuscript reports the study results.

claim: The number of index cases that were part of a household outbreak increased from 66.4% before the intervention to 80.3% after the intervention.
source: The number of index cases that were part of a household outbreak increased from 66.4% before the intervention to 80.3% after the intervention.
evidence: The manuscript reports the study results.

claim: Weekly average contact tracing delay decreased while the percentage of known sources of infection increased in the period after intervention implementation.
source: Weekly average contact tracing delay decreased while the percentage of known sources of infection increased in the period after intervention implementation (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the study results with reference to a figure.

claim: Known sources of infection (IRR 0.75 95% CI 0.63–0.91) was associated with the decrease of the number of secondary cases.
source: Results of negative binomial regression covering the entire period show that both known sources of infection (IRR 0.75 95% CI 0.63–0.91) and decrease in tracing delay (1/IRR 0.97 95% CI 0.94–1.01 for each day of avoided delay) were associated with the decrease of the number of secondary cases (Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical results with reference to a table.

claim: Decrease in tracing delay (1/IRR 0.97 95% CI 0.94–1.01 for each day of avoided delay) was associated with the decrease of the number of secondary cases.
source: Results of negative binomial regression covering the entire period show that both known sources of infection (IRR 0.75 95% CI 0.63–0.91) and decrease in tracing delay (1/IRR 0.97 95% CI 0.94–1.01 for each day of avoided delay) were associated with the decrease of the number of secondary cases (Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical results with reference to a table.

claim: Sensitivity analyses restricted to the period before the spread of the Alpha variant showed similar results.
source: Sensitivity analyses restricted to the period before the spread of the Alpha variant showed similar results (Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of sensitivity analysis with reference to a table.

claim: Only the known source of infection of the index case was associated with the outcome in multivariable analysis.
source: Only the known source of infection of the index case was associated with the outcome (number of secondary cases) in multivariable analysis and it was, therefore, tested for the mediation and interaction in the four-way decomposition method.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of multivariable analysis.

claim: The direct effect of the intervention accounted for a large part of the excess in risk (excess relative risk –0.29 95%–0.61– 0.03).
source: The direct effect of the intervention accounted for the large part of the excess in risk (excess relative risk –0.29 95%–0.61– 0.03), leading to the 29% decrease in the number of secondary cases if the source of infection of the index case is known.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of mediation analysis.

claim: Interaction only accounted for the other large part of the excess risk (excess relative risk 0.35 95% 0.03–0.68).
source: Interaction only accounted for the other large part of the excess risk (excess relative risk 0.35 95% 0.03–0.68); knowing the source of infection of the index case in the period before the intervention when tracing delay was high, would increase the risk of secondary cases by 35%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of mediation analysis.

claim: Knowing the source of infection of the index case in the period before the intervention when tracing delay was high would increase the risk of secondary cases by 35%.
source: Interaction only accounted for the other large part of the excess risk (excess relative risk 0.35 95% 0.03–0.68); knowing the source of infection of the index case in the period before the intervention when tracing delay was high, would increase the risk of secondary cases by 35%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of mediation analysis with interpretation.

claim: There was evidence of mediated interaction that had a negative effect on the secondary transmission (excess relative risk –0.14 95% CI –0.28–0.01).
source: However, we found evidence of mediated interaction that had a negative effect on the secondary transmission (excess relative risk –0.14 95% CI –0.28–0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of mediation analysis.

claim: The known source of infection of the index case alone accounted for only a small percent of the reduction of excess risk (excess relative risk –0.02 95% –0.10–0.07).
source: The known source of infection of the index case alone accounted for only a small percent of the reduction of excess risk (excess relative risk –0.02 95% –0.10–0.07).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of mediation analysis.

claim: The findings are consistent with modeling studies reporting that contact tracing efficacy decreases sharply with increasing delays between symptom onset and tracing.
source: Our findings are consistent with those of modeling studies reporting that contact tracing efficacy decreases sharply with increasing delays between symptom onset and tracing and with a lower fraction of symptomatic infections being tested, fewer cases ascertained by contact tracing, and increasing transmission before symptom onset (Kretzschmar et al., 2020; Gardner and Kilpatrick, 2021; Bradshaw et al., 2021; Hellewell et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript compares the study findings to prior modeling studies with citations.

claim: A previous modeling study showed that identifying positive cases within 5 days after exposure to their infector could reduce by 30% onward transmission at schools.
source: Moreover, our previous modelling study showed that identifying positive cases within 5 days after exposure to their infector could reduce by 30% onward transmission at schools (Molina Grané et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior modeling study.

claim: Observational studies demonstrated that various improvements in contact tracing can reduce the secondary transmission or even mortality in the community.
source: Observational studies also demonstrated that various improvements in contact tracing (Malheiro et al., 2020) can reduce the secondary transmission or even mortality in the community (Vecino-Ortiz et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites observational studies.

claim: Open-label and field trials showed that daily testing and twice-a-week testing strategies are effective in limiting the secondary transmission while reducing the loss of in-person school days.
source: A few open-label and field trials conducted with intention to minimize confounding showed that daily testing and twice-a-week testing strategies are effective in limiting the secondary transmission while reducing the loss of in-person school days (Young et al., 2021; Harris-McCoy et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites trial studies.

claim: The effectiveness of contact tracing highly depends on the number of cases being traced.
source: It has been shown that the effectiveness of contact tracing highly depends on the number of cases being traced, i.e., it decreases when the burden of new cases is too high for the tracing capacity of the health services (Gardner and Kilpatrick, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study about contact tracing effectiveness.

claim: BCT is more effective when community transmission is low to moderate.
source: In fact, BCT is more effective when community transmission is low to moderate (Ontario Agency for Health Protection and Promotion (Public Health Ontario), 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a public health guidance document.

claim: Increased new cases burden and high transmission during the winter months could be factors that might have minimised the true effect of the intervention.
source: Similarly, increased new cases burden and high transmission during the winter months in our study could be factors that might have minimised the true effect of the intervention.
evidence: This is an inference about potential confounding in the study.

claim: Before the intervention, most classes were put in quarantine immediately independently of the presence of secondary transmission in the class.
source: First, before the intervention, most classes were put in quarantine immediately independently of the presence of secondary transmission in the class, considering all classmates as close contacts, thus, delay in testing was not relevant for secondary transmission in these classes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the practices before the intervention.

claim: The unmeasured tracing delay in the family/community better reflects the intervention efficacy and represents the timeliness in linking SARS-CoV-2 positive children to the school investigation.
source: Furthermore, the unmeasured tracing delay in the family/community better reflects the intervention efficacy and represents the timeliness in linking SARS-CoV-2 positive children to the school investigation.
evidence: This is an inference about what the unmeasured variable represents.

claim: A better link between sporadic cases in households to school exposure after the intervention implementation is supported by the higher fraction of asymptomatic index cases identified.
source: A better link between sporadic cases in households to school exposure after the intervention implementation is also supported by the higher fraction of asymptomatic index cases identified as well as the higher fraction of index cases that were part of a household cluster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study data.

claim: A better link between sporadic cases in households to school exposure after the intervention implementation is supported by the higher fraction of index cases that were part of a household cluster.
source: A better link between sporadic cases in households to school exposure after the intervention implementation is also supported by the higher fraction of asymptomatic index cases identified as well as the higher fraction of index cases that were part of a household cluster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study data.

claim: The direct effect of the intervention would lead to an almost 30% reduction in secondary transmission if the source of infection of all index cases was known.
source: The direct effect of the intervention would lead to an almost 30% reduction in secondary transmission if the source of infection of all index cases was known.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results.

claim: The known source of infection had a greater impact on the secondary transmission when acting in the interaction with the intervention than independently (14% vs 2% reduction in the number of secondary cases).
source: Moreover, the known source of infection had a greater impact on the secondary transmission when acting in the interaction with the intervention than independently (14% vs 2% reduction in the number of secondary cases).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results.

claim: Before the intervention, knowing the source of infection for the school index case was often identified during the field investigation and not before.
source: This possibly reflects that, before the intervention, often the source of infection for the school index case was identified during the field investigation and not before, thus, in the absence of BCT, knowing the source of infection is not a sign of timeliness at all.
evidence: This is an inference about the meaning of the process indicator before the intervention.

claim: In the absence of BCT, knowing the source of infection is not a sign of timeliness.
source: This possibly reflects that, before the intervention, often the source of infection for the school index case was identified during the field investigation and not before, thus, in the absence of BCT, knowing the source of infection is not a sign of timeliness at all.
evidence: This is an inference about the meaning of the process indicator.

claim: The major limitation of the study is its before-and-after design.
source: The major limitation of the study is its before-and-after design; i.e., the impossibility to make an inference that observed changes are due to intervention and not due to other factors.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a methodological limitation.

claim: It is impossible to make an inference that observed changes are due to intervention and not due to other factors in a before-and-after design.
source: The major limitation of the study is its before-and-after design; i.e., the impossibility to make an inference that observed changes are due to intervention and not due to other factors.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: Multivariate and mediation analysis may not be enough to control for the fact that the force of infection was changing over the time series.
source: In fact, multivariate and mediation analysis may not be enough to control for the fact that the force of infection was changing over the time series.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the analytical approach.

claim: It is often impossible to conduct properly designed experimental studies under a public health emergency.
source: It is often impossible to conduct properly designed experimental studies under a public health emergency.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of research during emergencies.

claim: It was impossible to apply the intervention to a limited number of schools because it was an intervention targeting household clusters during the peak of the second pandemic wave.
source: Nevertheless, it was impossible to apply our intervention to a limited number of schools, because it was an intervention targeting household clusters, in a particularly critical moment, i.e., during the peak of the second pandemic wave.
evidence: The manuscript explains why a randomized design was not feasible.

source: The only way to assess the effectiveness of this intervention was to design an observational study trying to minimise the effect of confounding.

source: A possible solution was testing the effect of mediators strictly linked to the intervention process (Accorsi et al., 2021).

source: We adjusted analyses for major sources of confounding, but there are still unmeasured confounders.

source: In fact, we could not classify the preventive measures put in place in each school, the time spent by each index case in the classroom, or the out-school contacts between classmates.

source: Another important limitation is the lack of testing delay in a family/community as a process indicator, that we consider one of the real mechanisms of action of the new tracing strategy (first gray part of the conceptual scheme), but we assume this delay in the community follows the same trend as the delay observed in schools.

source: Lastly, the same intervention may not yield the same results in a different epidemiological context, such as the presence of other variants of the virus (Omicron), or different control measures.

claim: This is the only study that attempted to quantify the potential effect of changing a contact tracing strategy in a community on secondary transmission in schools.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only study that attempted to quantify the potential effect of changing a contact tracing strategy in a community on secondary transmission in schools by estimating the excess risk associated with the intervention, through the application of a new mediation analysis method which allowed us to partition the total excess risk into separate effects of the intervention and its process indicators in the presence of their interaction (VanderWeele, 2014; Discacciati et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty of the study with citations.

claim: The study applied a new mediation analysis method which allowed partitioning the total excess risk into separate effects of the intervention and its process indicators in the presence of their interaction.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only study that attempted to quantify the potential effect of changing a contact tracing strategy in a community on secondary transmission in schools by estimating the excess risk associated with the intervention, through the application of a new mediation analysis method which allowed us to partition the total excess risk into separate effects of the intervention and its process indicators in the presence of their interaction (VanderWeele, 2014; Discacciati et al., 2019).

claim: The study can have important methodological implications.
source: As such it can have important methodological implications as well.

claim: Changing the contact tracing strategy in the community reduced the time of contact tracing.
source: Changing the contact tracing strategy in the community, from testing contacts at the end of quarantine to testing contacts immediately, reduced the time of contact tracing and increased the ability to identify the source of infection in school outbreaks.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study data.

claim: Changing the contact tracing strategy in the community increased the ability to identify the source of infection in school outbreaks.
source: Changing the contact tracing strategy in the community, from testing contacts at the end of quarantine to testing contacts immediately, reduced the time of contact tracing and increased the ability to identify the source of infection in school outbreaks.

claim: The improvement in tracing performance appears to be linked to a decrease in the number of secondary cases in school contacts.
source: The improvement in tracing performance appears to be linked to a decrease in the number of secondary cases in school contacts, although the intervention was implemented in a changing context just after the incidence peak of the autumn wave, and we cannot exclude that the observed differences are due to differences in the force of infection and to other control measures put in place before as the reduction of in presence school attendance.
evidence: This is a cautious conclusion acknowledging limitations.

source: (A) In standard contact tracing, all close contacts were quarantined after identifying a case in the community. Contacts were only tested at the end of the quarantine or if symptomatic.

source: (A) In standard contact tracing, all close contacts were quarantined after identifying a case in the community. Contacts were only tested at the end of the quarantine or if symptomatic.

source: Only for school contacts, immediate testing of all classmates was performed; if one or more classmates resulted positive, the whole class was quarantined.

source: Only for school contacts, immediate testing of all classmates was performed; if one or more classmates resulted positive, the whole class was quarantined.
